title: Social news feed
prompt: Design the home feed for a social network with 200 million daily active users. Each user follows about 200 accounts, and a few thousand celebrities have more than 10 million followers each. Users publish 100 million posts a day and open their feed about 10 times a day. The feed shows posts from the accounts a user follows, newest first, and must load in under 300 ms. A new post should appear in followers' feeds within a minute.
explanation: Pushing every post into every follower's feed makes reads fast, until a celebrity with ten million followers posts. What it tests is seeing that, and combining push for most accounts with pull for the few huge ones.

requirements: Covers the feed of followed accounts, newest first with pagination, plus posting and following
Puts numbers on feed latency (under 300 ms) and freshness (a minute), and accepts eventual consistency
Calls out celebrity accounts as the case that breaks a naive design
estimation: About 2 billion feed reads a day, over 20,000 a second on average, and about 1,200 posts a second
Pushing every post to 200 followers is about 20 billion feed inserts a day, and one celebrity post alone is over 10 million
Keeping the latest few hundred post ids for each user is hundreds of gigabytes, which fits a sharded cache
api_data_model: GET /feed with a cursor rather than an offset, and POST /posts
Posts keyed by a time-sortable id (Snowflake-style), follows stored in both directions, and a per-user feed list of post ids
Feeds hold post ids that are hydrated from a post cache, not copies of the posts
architecture: Fan-out on write for ordinary accounts: async workers push a new post id into each follower's feed list
Fan-out on read for celebrities: their recent posts are merged into the feed when it is read
A feed service reading the feed cache, with post and social graph services behind it
scalability: A hybrid of push and pull, switched on a follower-count threshold
A feed cache sharded by user id and capped at a few hundred entries per user
Skips fan-out to inactive users and builds their feed on demand when they return
reliability: Weighs fan-out on write (fast reads, heavy writes) against fan-out on read (cheap writes, slow reads) explicitly
Queues fan-out work so a surge of posts delays feeds slightly instead of failing posts
Rebuilds a lost feed cache from the follows and posts tables
communication: Follows one ordinary post and one celebrity post through to a follower's feed
Uses the estimates to justify where the push and pull threshold sits
